pll1d3c2-d1e3476.summary: Turns from vestiges in creatures to the image of the Trinity in the human mind, which knows or can know God.
claims: The image of the Trinity is found in the human mind.

pll1d3c2-d1e3491.summary: With De Trinitate XIV, locates the image in the mind, the best thing in our nature: the mind is God's image because it is capable of and can participate in God, and remains an image even when deformed. Its remembering, understanding, and loving itself form a trinity, not yet God but God's image.
claims: The image of God is in the mind.
The mind is God's image because it is capable of God.
The image remains even when participation in God is lost.
Memory, understanding, and love of self form a trinity in the mind.

pll1d3c2-d1e3524.summary: With De Trinitate X: memory, understanding, and will are one life, one mind, one essence; they are three insofar as they are said relatively to one another, and what is said of each absolutely is said in the singular.
claims: Memory, understanding, and will are one life, mind, and essence.
They are three by relation to one another.
Absolute predicates of them are said in the singular.
concepts: unity and trinity in the mind

pll1d3c2-d1e3545.summary: Argues that the three are equal, each to each and each to all, because they mutually comprehend: I remember that I have memory, understanding, and will; whatever I understand or will I know and therefore remember, so I remember the whole of each.
claims: Memory, understanding, and will are equal, each to each and each to all.
Memory contains the whole of memory, understanding, and will.

pll1d3c2-d1e3557.summary: Continues: understanding grasps all three wholly, since what I do not understand I neither remember nor will.
claims: Whatever is remembered and willed is understood.

pll1d3c2-d1e3569.summary: Completes the argument: will takes in all of understanding and memory by using all it understands and remembers, so each whole is equal to each and to all, and the three are one life, mind, and essence.
claims: The will comprehends the whole of understanding and memory.
Each of the three is equal to each and to all together.

pll1d3c2-d1e3581.summary: Concludes that the human mind is an unequal image of the supreme Unity and Trinity. Clarifies terms: 'mind' here means the soul, though properly it means what is most excellent in the soul; and memory concerns present as well as absent and past things, or it could not grasp itself.
claims: The human mind is an image, though unequal, of the Trinity.
'Mind' properly names what is more excellent in the soul.
Memory is also of present things.

pll1d3c2-d1e3630.summary: Raises a difficulty: taken properly, the claim that the three are one mind and one essence seems false, since the mind is a spiritual substance while memory, understanding, and will are its natural powers, which differ from one another.
claims: Properly speaking, memory, understanding, and will are natural powers of the mind and differ from one another.

pll1d3c2-d1e3633.summary: Adds Augustine that the three are referred to themselves and are inseparable: the mind cannot love or remember itself unless it knows itself, and yet each and all are one essence even though said relatively to one another.
claims: The mind cannot love or remember what it does not know.
The three are inseparable and yet one essence.

pll1d3c2-d1e3663.summary: Gives Lombard's resolution: the three are called one substance because they exist substantially in the soul, not as accidents that can come and go in a subject.
claims: Memory, understanding, and will are called one substance because they exist substantially in the mind.
They are not accidents in a subject.

pll1d3c2-d1e3666.summary: Supports the resolution with De Trinitate IX: these exist substantially in the mind and not as in a subject, like color in a body; though relative to one another, each is substantially in its substance.
claims: The three exist in the mind substantially, not as color in a body.

pll1d3c2-d1e3688.summary: Closes the explanation and, with De Trinitate XV, notes the mind's dignity: through memory, understanding, and love it can recall, behold, and desire the eternal and unchangeable nature, and anyone who perceives this finds the image of the supreme Trinity.
claims: Through memory, understanding, and love the mind can recall, behold, and embrace the eternal nature.
In this the mind finds the image of the supreme Trinity.

pl-l1d3c2.summary: Seeks the image of the Trinity in the human mind, following Augustine's De Trinitate. The mind is God's image because it is capable of God, even when deformed. Its memory, understanding, and will are one life, one mind, one essence, yet three by their mutual relations, and each comprehends all and each is equal to all. Lombard then raises a difficulty: properly the three are natural powers distinct from each other, not the mind's essence. He resolves it by saying they are called one substance because they exist substantially in the soul, not as accidents in a subject. Through these powers the mind remembers, sees, and loves the eternal nature, and so finds the image of the supreme Trinity.
claims: The image of the Trinity is to be found in the mind, the best part of human nature.
The mind is God's image because it is capable of God, even when deformed by sin.
Memory, understanding, and will are one life, mind, and essence, and three by mutual relation.
Each of the three comprehends the others and all, so they are equal.
Memory, understanding, and will are called one substance because they exist substantially in the soul, not as accidents.
Through memory, understanding, and love the mind can recall, behold, and embrace the eternal nature.
